perspective:
Harold’s available information:

- He is a project manager and has a friendly/professional relationship with Arthur; he seeks Arthur’s advice when stressed.
- He feels frustrated and anxious because his project team seems unmotivated, affecting progress. He meets Arthur at a coffee shop.
- He hears Arthur advise: motivation is tricky; understand what drives each team member individually; have one-on-one conversations; people need to feel valued and understood.
- Afterward, Harold feels hopeful and relieved. He tells his team he wants one-on-one chats to understand their motivations. He hears TM1 say it could be helpful and TM2 say they are open to it. He schedules time and says they will make the project a success together.
- Later, Harold observes the team still not responding well and feels disappointed/worried. He tells Arthur this.
- He hears Arthur suggest there may be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors; Harold should dig deeper. Harold says he will set up another round of meetings.
- Harold holds one-on-one meetings. TM1 tells him there is tension between a few people affecting work. TM2 tells him they feel overwhelmed by the workload and stressed, making motivation hard. Harold says he will look into resolving conflicts and possibly redistribute tasks, and that TM2’s well-being is important.
- Harold feels optimistic and empowered. He tells the team they will have regular feedback sessions and team-building activities to create a more supportive environment. TM1 says it sounds great and will help; TM2 agrees and says it is good concerns are being addressed. Harold says he is glad and emphasizes working together, input, and well-being.
